extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of reflective/personal essays; students of philosophy and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative norms for composing or judging reflective, personal essays (à la Montaigne) emphasizing self-examination, clarity, prudence, and experiential authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of experience as a path to knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “Where reason is wanting, we therein employ experience… which is a means much more weak and cheap; but truth is so great a thing that we ought not to disdain any mediation that will guide us to it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat experience as a legitimate (if imperfect) mediator of truth when pure reason cannot decide; do not disdain experiential evidence even if it is weaker than abstract reasoning. Use concrete trials and examples to inform judgment, but remain conscious of their limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about generalizing from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: “Reason has so many forms that we know not to which to take; experience has no fewer; the consequence we would draw from the comparison of events is unsure… There is no quality so universal in this image of things as diversity and variety.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing conclusions from events or examples, acknowledge variability and the imperfection of analogy; avoid asserting universal laws from limited or diverse experiential instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer few, simple, and general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most to be desired are those that are the most rare, the most simple and general; and I am even of opinion that we had better have none at all than to have them in so prodigious a number as we have.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value legal/institutional rules that are general and simple; beware proliferation of special-case rules which increase ambiguity and disputes. Practical implication: prefer brevity and generality over extensive technical subdivision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-technical, artificial language in law and contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: “The princes of that art… have so weighed every syllable, and so thoroughly sifted every sort of quirking connection that they are now confounded and entangled… As you see children trying to bring a mass of quicksilver to a certain number of parts, the more they press and work it the more it irritates the liberty of this generous metal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain intelligible language in wills, contracts, and similar documents; excessive hair-splitting phrasing creates confusion and multiplies disputes. Anti-pattern: drafting with arcane subtleties that obfuscate rather than clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of excessive commentary and scholastic subdivision
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is more ado to interpret interpretations than to interpret things, and more books upon books than upon any other subject; we do nothing but comment upon one another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor direct exposition of ideas over multiplying glosses and commentaries. Excessive secondary interpretation tends to increase doubt rather than clarifying primary texts. When evaluating scholarship or exposition, reward clarity and original thought rather than mere commentary proliferation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware definitional proliferation
rubrics_metrics.description: “We exchange one word for another, and often for one less understood. To satisfy one doubt, they give me three; ‘tis the Hydra’s head.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid solving a terminological problem by introducing more obscure or numerous definitions. Aim for definitions that reduce confusion and are practically useful; resist splitting concepts into many subtypes unless necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogies and comparisons cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every example halts, and the relation which is drawn from experience is always faulty and imperfect. Comparisons are ever-coupled at one end or other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using examples or analogies, explicitly acknowledge their limits and the non-identity between cases. Do not treat an illustrative comparison as proof of full equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mercy and human sympathy over strict punitive justice
rubrics_metrics.description: “When occasion has required me to sentence criminals, I have rather chosen to fail in point of justice than to do it… The deformity of the first cruelty makes me abhor all imitation of it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging others, especially in punitive contexts, weigh the human consequences of strict application of rules; favor clemency where the harm of punishment or rigid sentence would be disproportionate. Example: the author would accept failing strict legalism rather than inflicting irreversible harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the fallibility and contradiction of human justice
rubrics_metrics.description: “What we find to be favour and severity in justice… human justice is formed after the model of physic, according to which, all that is useful is also just and honest… there is nothing so much, nor so grossly, nor so ordinarily faulty, as the laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating legal or institutional outcomes, account for systemic error, contradiction, and the social contingency of laws. Do not presume laws always embody fairness; treat them as human constructs subject to reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward and recognize good service as well as punish bad
rubrics_metrics.description: “In China… the officers deputed by the prince… as they punish those who behave themselves ill in their charge, so do they liberally reward those who have conducted themselves better than the common sort.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design and practice should include positive incentives and public recognition for exceptional service, not only punitive measures. This fosters better conduct and morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know thyself: introspection as primary practical learning
rubrics_metrics.description: “I study myself more than any other subject; ‘tis my metaphysic, my physic… To my weakness… I owe the propension I have to modesty, to the obedience of belief prescribed me, to a constant coldness and moderation of opinions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical wisdom and improved judgement, prioritize sustained self-examination. Learning from one’s own errors provides lasting correction and humility; this is more directly useful to life than abstract study alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal experience of error to temper confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “When I find myself convinced, by the reason of another, of a false opinion, I do not so much learn what he has said… as, in general, I learn my own debility and the treachery of my understanding… I learn to suspect my steps throughout.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn instances of being corrected into general lessons about the unreliability of one’s judgment; cultivate suspicion of confident belief and readiness to revise. This is an epistemic virtue to be sought in writers and thinkers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep judgment distinct from and uncorrupted by passions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Judgment holds in me a magisterial seat; at least it carefully endeavours to make it so: it leaves my appetites to take their own course… if it cannot reform the other parts… at least it suffers not itself to be corrupted by them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a deliberative faculty that can observe passions without being captured by them. In practical writing or decision-making, signal when you are reporting impulses versus when you are giving reasoned judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dogmatic affirmation and obstinacy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Affirmation and obstinacy are express signs of want of wit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value tentative, questioning tone over assertive dogmatism. In argumentation and exposition, prefer humility and openness to correction; penalize rhetorical stubbornness as a sign of intellectual weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-knowledge improves judgment of others
rubrics_metrics.description: “That long attention that I employ in considering myself, also fits me to judge tolerably enough of others… By having from my infancy been accustomed to contemplate my own life in those of others, I have acquired a complexion studious in that particular.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate introspective habits to enhance empathy and acuity in judging others. When evaluating people’s behavior, use your own documented experience as a comparative lens rather than relying solely on external theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor direct, piece-by-piece experimental exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: “The wise speak and deliver their fancies more specifically, and piece by piece; I… present mine generally without rule and experimentally: I pronounce my opinion by disjointed articles, as a thing that cannot be spoken at once and in gross.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For personal or reflective writing, clarity can be achieved by presenting observations in discrete, concrete fragments and experiments rather than forcing a grand systematic structure. Value experiential fragments and illustrative vignettes.
